items.summary_en: Can a logged dataset visit every hidden state frequently and still be exponentially uninformative about a target policy's value? items.title: Playing log(N)-Questions over Wikipedia Abstracts: Communication Efficiency Between Paired Frontier Models
items.summary_en: We evaluate six frontier language models on the two-agent $\log(N)$-Questions game. items.title: Coupled Calibration and Learning: Mitigating Teacher Bias in LLM Distillation without Target-Domain Reward Feedback
items.summary_en: Large language model (LLM) distillation aims to transfer the capabilities of a powerful teacher to a smaller student. Direct imitation, however, can also transfer the teacher's systematic bias and errors. This challenge is particularly pronounced under covariate shift, when the teacher's reliability on target questions is uncertain and target-domain reward feedback is unavailable. We propose Coupled Calibration and Learning (CCL), an LLM distillation algorithm that couples teacher calibration with student updates through token-level branching, using reward feedback only on source questions. items.title: A humorous social-affective instructional style in generative AI pedagogical agents: effects on cognitive load, immediate learning performance, and learner perceptions
items.summary_en: Generative AI pedagogical agents can provide adaptive instructional dialogue, but their responses may also appear impersonal, overly formal, or insufficiently engaging. One possible design response is to embed instructionally relevant humor into agent–learner interaction. This study examined whether a humorous social-affective instructional style that combined content-related, non-disparaging humor with mild colloquial expression and encouraging language influenced learners’ self-reported cognitive load, immediate post-test performance, and perceived agent value in an online learning activity.

For GEM, it combines records of sponsored placements with notice probabilities. GMMM compares expected business response

items.title: Can Foundation Models Moderate Online Content? Evaluating Instruction- vs. Example-Driven Policy Operationalization
items.summary_en: The growing complexity of content moderation policies presents a critical challenge for their consistent operationalization. While foundation models possess the basic capabilities needed to confront this challenge, whether they can reliably moderate online content remains an unanswered question. In this paper, we systematically compare two competing paradigms for Vision-Language Model (VLM) guidance: an instruction-driven approach where models reason from policy precepts, and an example-driven approach where they generalize from prior precedents. We ground this investigation in ModerationBench
